transcript:
[00:00] Lena (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time today. Quick intros, we're focused on an Optimize walkthrough — batching, prefix/KV prefetch and cost model.
[00:12] Priya: Thanks, excited. We're trying to get cost predictability for our conversational assistants, plus keep 95th perc latency under 350ms.
[00:25] Jason (SE): Great. Marcus, do you want to give a quick overview of your workload shape? average tokens, session length, concurrency?
[00:35] Marcus: Sure — most sessions are 8 to 14 turns, average generation 120 tokens, heavy tail up to 800 tokens for support transcripts. Peak concurrency right now is about 120 QPS but that's global; per-region 40 to 60.
[00:52] Lena: OK so medium-length sessions with occasional long tails. That maps well to prefix cache opportunities.
[01:10] Sara: Quick question — what exactly is prefix vs KV cache again? I remember KV is like the key-value cache of past key/values?
[01:18] Jason: Yeah, quick primer: prefix cache is caching token prefixes for repeated starts — good for templated prompts. KV cache stores decoder KV state for session continuation which lets you prefetch and resume without recomputing earlier layers. Prefetching KV for hot sessions reduces per-token compute a lot.
[01:40] Priya: Does prefetching increase memory? how much overhead?
[01:44] Jason: It increases transient memory—KV cache for a long context could be tens to hundreds of MB per session depending on model size and quantization. We showed quantization profiles in the deck — lower-precision halves KV size for many models, but there are perf tradeoffs.
[02:05] Marcus: How do you pick TTL for prefix entries? we have low churn for onboarding flows, but organic chat is more variable.
[02:12] Jason: TTL is workload-driven — for onboarding templates you can set longer TTLs, maybe 24–72h. For organic chat you'll want short TTLs, like minutes, and rely more on session-based KV. Redwood Optimize suggests TTLs by cluster of route patterns.
[02:33] Lena: We have a saved simulation (cost_model_v3.xlsx) that we'll tailor with your prompt set. That shows cost sensitivity across batch sizes and cache hit rates.
[02:45] Priya: Can you walk the cost model quickly? the tradeoff I've heard is latency vs per-token cost, but curious about autoscale bursts.
[02:55] Jason: Sure — row-by-row: x-axis is concurrency / throughput, y-axis is per-token unit cost. With caching + prefetch you collapse the compute curve a lot. If you prefetch top-10 sessions you can save up to 30–45% unit cost in our sim, depending on hit-rate.
[03:18] Marcus: Is that savings assuming Dedicated or Hosted?
[03:22] Jason: The spreadsheet contrasts Hosted per-token blended pricing vs Dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commit amortized). Dedicated wins when sustained throughput is high and latency SLO is strict. Hosted is better for spiky and low-volume.
[03:34] Owen: For Dedicated, what's the scale steps? our infra team has network egress caps, and we need to know node counts.
[03:41] Jason: Typical m60-equivalent pool: start at 4 nodes, autoscale to 12 for bursts. We can model a mixed policy: reserve baseline 4 nodes and allow burst autoscale; billing reflects reserved + burst.
[03:55] Priya: Security — how do you handle keys and our KMS? we need HSM/KMS integration and audit logs.
[04:03] Lena: Redwood Private supports customer KMS via Cloud KMS or on-prem HSM; audit logs and per-request trace are supported. We'll attach SOC2_summary.pdf and our KMS integration notes.
[04:20] Sara: For the POC, what's the simplest setup to show batch + KV prefetch savings?
[04:26] Jason: Run a 24-48h simulation with your prompt set: two lanes — baseline (no prefetch, small batch) vs optimized (prefix prefetch + KV for top sessions, larger batch window). Measure token cost, 95th latency, and model quality. We can run it on Dedicated test pool or a Hosted test endpoint.
[04:48] Marcus: Any pitfalls — like query variability causing cache thrash?
[04:52] Jason: Yes — high churn can reduce hit rate. That's why we cluster sessions via fingerprinting and only prefetch hot session candidates. Also adaptive TTLs help. There's a small risk of wasted prefetch compute if mispredicted, but our cost-model accounts for a misprediction penalty.
[05:10] Priya: Can the runtime fallback to a smaller model if latency spikes? we want graceful degradation.
[05:15] Lena: Yes, smart routing can fallback to a compatible quantized or distilled variant. You can configure fallbacks by latency tier or cost tier.
[05:26] Owen: Network — what's egress effect from KV? do you ship KV over wire?
[05:31] Jason: No, KV cache is local to the serving instance. For Private deployments within your VPC it's all internal, no cross-region egress. For Hosted there is regional routing; we avoid extra egress for cached sessions.
[05:48] Marcus: Walk me through an example calculation for a 120-token completion with and without KV prefetch.
[05:54] Jason: Without prefetch: full forward passes for all tokens -> X FLOPs -> baseline cost. With KV prefetch: you precompute encoder and early decoder layers once, then incremental token generation is much cheaper — in our sim that cut per-token compute by ~55% for that shape. Exact numbers in the cost_model_v3.xlsx.
[06:17] Priya: What about batching — what's the ideal batch size? my worry is latency for interactive flows.
[06:23] Jason: There's a latency envelope: small batches (2–8) keep tail latency low but miss some GPU saturation; medium (8–24) better throughput but added queue time. Redwood Optimize recommends adaptive batching: small batch for low-latency routes, aggressive batching for background or async routes. We showed sample latency vs batch-size curves in the deck.
[06:45] Sara: Do you do request coalescing across customers — shared batching?
[06:49] Jason: No cross-tenant mixing for Dedicated; Hosted uses tenant-aware batching respecting isolation. Coalescing is within route/tenant groups to keep fairness.
[06:58] Priya: Pricing ask — can you show a blended sample with our expected 40 rps per region?
[07:03] Lena: We'll run the scenario in cost_model_v3 and return a tailored blended view; that's part of the follow-up.
[07:10] Marcus: About measuring quality — do you have eval hooks? we need to ensure prefetch doesn't regress output.
[07:16] Aria (Product): We integrate prompt-set evals and regression alerts. You can tie evals to rollouts so any quantization or model swap triggers a quality check.
[07:27] Priya: Good. For the POC, do you need us to whitelist IPs or open VPN?
[07:31] Owen: We prefer VPC peering if possible.
[07:34] Jason: For Dedicated, we can do VPC peering and private endpoints. For Hosted test endpoints we can use IP whitelist or private link. We'll document network steps in the runbook link.
[07:48] Marcus: One more — what's the control plane visibility for cache metrics? can we see hit-rate per route?
[07:53] Jason: Yes — Redwood Console exposes per-route cache hit-rate, TTL distribution, batch latency, cost per-token. We'll give you a demo dashboard for your routes during the POC.
[08:05] Priya: Any examples of customers who landed 30%+ savings?
[08:09] Lena: Several customers in retail and support with repetitive templates saw 25–40% unit-cost reduction after prefix + KV prefetch and batching tuning. We'll anonymize specific case studies and share.
[08:22] Sara: Are there specific model families you recommend for better KV efficiency?
[08:26] Jason: Models with optimized attention kernels and long-context support perform best. Also 8-bit and 4-bit quant profiles can help but require quality validation; Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles per workload.
[08:39] Priya: Let's talk POC scope real quick — metrics and success criteria?
[08:44] Lena: Success: >20% per-token cost reduction vs baseline while preserving model quality (A/B pass rate) and maintaining 95th latency under 350ms. Reporting: cost delta, hit-rate, latency distribution, and memory usage.
[08:58] Marcus: Do you support injection of synthetic load for realistic concurrency?
[09:02] Jason: Yes, we can run synthetic traffic shaped by your real traces. If you provide a sample trace, we'll replay it for the POC.
[09:12] Priya: Timeline — we want results in 2 weeks. Is that realistic?
[09:16] Jason: Two weeks is tight but possible for a light POC: gather prompts this week, run bench next week, deliver results by end of week two. Dedicated provisioning might add lead time if you need reserved capacity.
[09:32] Lena: We'll summarize the plan in email; action items below.
[09:36] Priya: Cool. A few nitty-gritty clarifications — how do you handle model version pinning during rollouts?
[09:41] Aria: You can pin routes to model versions and run canaries. If quality regresses, automatic rollback can be triggered based on eval hooks.
[09:51] Owen: On the Dedicated billing, can bursts be limited to a budget? we don't want runaway cost.
[09:56] Lena: Yes, you can set burst caps and alerting thresholds. Billing reflects actual usage and we can configure budget caps.
[10:08] Marcus: For the run we'll want per-token cost broken down by compute, storage, and orchestration overhead if possible.
[10:13] Jason: We'll provide a breakdown; console exposes token-level cost buckets.
[10:20] Priya: Anything else?
[10:23] Sara: Not from product.
[10:25] Lena: Ok quick recap of next steps — Lena will send tailored cost_model_v3.xlsx; Jason will schedule the benchmark; Priya will share prompt set and traces; Owen will provide VPC/egress details. We'll aim for initial POC data by 2026-07-09.
[10:44] Priya: Thanks, appreciate the practical approach.
[10:48] Lena: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.
[10:52] Marcus: Thanks.
